plot_extraction.response_text:
A hardworking, deaf narrator spends a hot day repairing and improving his rented home, then meticulously prepares an elaborate hot bath. He heats the water, rigs a canvas steam cover and headrest, lays out toiletries, reading material, clean clothes, coffee, and food, and carefully carries boiling water to the tub. Only when he steps in does he discover that all the water has drained away because he forgot to insert the plug.

Exhausted and disappointed, he abandons the bath and falls asleep in his dirty work clothes. He compares this simple but disastrous oversight to the lives of the impoverished, transient residents of a nearby terrace: many people begin life confidently and plan carefully, yet fail because of one neglected essential detail, sometimes through physical disadvantages beyond their control.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story uses a conversational, digressive first-person style that combines urban observation, comic anecdote, and explicit moral reflection. The narrator speaks directly and informally, often seeming to think aloud as he moves between the shabby terrace opposite his balcony, his pleasure in manual work, and the elaborate preparations for his bath. Asides such as “you know,” self-corrections, parenthetical remarks, and abrupt qualifications create the impression of spontaneous speech rather than tightly controlled literary narration. The voice is personable and self-deprecating, but also sharply observant, socially conscious, and prone to turning ordinary details into broader reflections on human life.

The tone blends dry humour, melancholy, affection, and irony. Poverty is depicted through grotesque comedy—the terrace resembles a row of skulls, with doors like tomahawk wounds—but the residents themselves are not treated with contempt. Repeated references to unpaid rent, improvised curtains, sudden removals, and anxious scrutiny of the rent collector establish deprivation without overt sentimentality. The narrator’s humour protects the material from becoming solemn while allowing an undercurrent of compassion to remain. His own failed bath is treated as farce, yet the final analogy transforms that farce into a sympathetic meditation on people whose lives have gone wrong, particularly those burdened by physical disadvantages.

The structure is deliberately loose and apparently disproportionate. A long opening description of “Skull Terrace” is openly declared to have “nothing whatever to do with the story,” after which the narrative shifts into an increasingly meticulous account of the narrator’s bath preparations. This apparent rambling is purposeful: the terrace supplies the social and moral frame, while the bath anecdote provides the comic emblem. Suspense arises not from danger but from exhaustive practical detail. Every item is arranged—the canvas, gas-pipe, towels, reading matter, tobacco, coffee, toast, toothbrush, and nail knife—before the revelation that the most basic necessity, the plug, has been forgotten. The final paragraphs then return to Skull Terrace and reinterpret the whole anecdote as an allegory of failed lives.

The prose alternates between long, accumulating sentences and short comic blows. Extended sentences pile up observations, objects, alternatives, and qualifications, mimicking both the narrator’s busy mind and his obsession with practical arrangements. Dashes and parentheses frequently interrupt the grammatical flow, adding jokes, corrections, or supplementary thoughts. Sentence fragments such as “Labours of love,” “Van of the ‘bottle ho’ variety,” and “But I was a carpenter and housepainter first” give the narration a spoken, anecdotal rhythm. Repetition is prominent: “ragged,” “casual,” “old,” and variations on vacancy recur until they become both comic motifs and social diagnoses. The climactic sentence, “I’d forgotten to put in the plug,” is extremely plain and brief, gaining force from its contrast with the elaborate preparation preceding it.

The diction mixes colloquial Australian speech, practical trade vocabulary, and mock-literary phrasing. Terms connected with building and household labour—“matchboard,” “galvanized iron,” “gas-pipe,” “limewashing,” “copper,” and nail sizes—lend tactile realism and establish the narrator as a working man who values competent manual craft. Informal expressions such as “pome,” “bottle ho,” and “knocked up” strengthen the vernacular voice. Against this plain diction, elevated phrases such as “pure and unadulterated joy,” “full glare of the day,” and “the sleep of utter happy weariness” are used partly sincerely and partly for comic inflation. The capitalised opening declaration, “THE MORAL should be revived,” parodies the conventions of openly didactic storytelling even as the narrative ultimately embraces them.

Imagery is concrete, visual, and often grotesquely personifying. The central image of the terrace as a skull gives the setting a deathly, hollow appearance, while its slit-like doors and furtive candlelight suggest precarious, half-visible lives. Domestic objects—old tablecloths, ragged blinds, buckets, canvas, string, towels, and scraps of wood—define a world of improvisation and scarcity. This material emphasis also supports the story’s moral logic: life depends upon small, practical details, and one missing component can render all other care useless. The bath plug consequently becomes a simple but flexible symbol for overlooked necessities, bad luck, human fallibility, and the hidden handicap that can undo otherwise intelligent effort.

Characterisation is achieved primarily through habits, objects, and gestures rather than psychological exposition. The terrace residents are sketched collectively through their furtive movements and makeshift possessions. The landlady is characterised through her peculiar thrift about firewood, her practical cooperation, and her excessive sympathy after the mishap. The narrator reveals himself through his deafness, pride in craftsmanship, delight in contrivance, appetite for comfort, and tendency to overprepare. His admission of physical impairment quietly complicates the joke and prepares the final reference to people “handicapped physically.”

Overall, the style is realist, vernacular, humorous, and morally reflective. It turns humble urban scenery and a trivial domestic failure into a social parable without abandoning the texture of ordinary life. Its characteristic movement is from comic particularity to humane generalisation: the reader first laughs at excessive preparation defeated by one omission, then is invited to see the same pattern in lives shaped by poverty, disability, circumstance, or mischance.

generation.response_text:
THE MORAL is out of fashion, I know. It went out with antimacassars, improving recitations, and those pictures of little girls crossing broken bridges in thunderstorms; but I have always thought it might be brought back in a plain working coat, without ribbons, and made useful again.

Opposite my balcony stood a row of houses called Mercy Terrace, though mercy had plainly passed along the other side of the street. In the hard afternoon light the place looked like a jawbone dug from a paddock—six yellowish houses, six black doorways, and windows that stared without seeing. Two panes were patched with brown paper. One had a flour-sack curtain printed BLUE ANCHOR BRAND, upside down. Another displayed half a lace curtain, as though respectability had started there and lost courage.

People were always moving into Mercy Terrace and always moving out. They came with bedding tied in rope, kerosene tins, perambulators containing everything except babies, and vans of the “bottle ho” variety. A proper furniture van never stopped there. It would have felt overdressed.

On moving-in day there was confidence. The woman scrubbed the step; the man carried a chair as if it were a throne; the children quarrelled over which corner belonged to whom. By the third week a sheet appeared in the window. By the fifth the rent collector appeared at the door. Then, generally at dusk, the bedding went back into the rope.

I used to watch these proceedings because I am deaf, and a deaf man becomes a great observer of doors. He cannot hear a knock, but he notices the instant tightening of a woman’s shoulders when one comes. He cannot hear the rent collector’s boots, but he sees curtains move in houses where no one is supposed to be home. Mercy Terrace was full of little betrayals of that kind—candlelight under a door, a child’s hand withdrawn from a window, smoke rising from a chimney whose tenant had declared the place empty.

This has nothing whatever to do with my bath.

At least, I thought so at the time.

The Saturday in question was hot enough to soften putty on the glass. I had been improving the house I rented, an occupation which landlords admire chiefly when they are not paying for it. The back room had a rotten strip of matchboard, the washhouse door hung down like a tired eyelid, and the fence possessed that free, independent motion usually associated with seaweed.

My landlady said the repairs were unnecessary.

“Nothing has fallen off yet,” she said.

I did not hear her, naturally, but she repeated it on a slate she kept for conversation with me. She was a considerate woman, though she wrote in very large letters, as if deafness were a failure of eyesight.

I replaced the matchboard, rehung the door, and put two new rails into the fence. Then, finding a tin of colour that had not entirely turned to pudding, I painted the washhouse. It was not a beautiful colour. It had begun life as green, had been mixed at some period with cream, and now resembled soup remembered from childhood. Still, it covered.

Labours of love.

There is pure and unadulterated joy in driving a nail straight, especially after living among people who put a three-inch nail where a screw ought to go and bend it over at the back for security. I worked through the full glare of the day, stopping only to drink water from the kitchen tap and to admire, from different angles, the improvements for which I should receive no reduction in rent.

By six o’clock I was striped with paint, sawdust, sweat, rust, and something black from beneath the washhouse that I did not investigate. My shirt could have stood in a corner by itself. My hands were not hands but exhibits. A wash at the basin would have been an insult. I determined upon a bath.

Not merely a bath, you understand. A bath properly conducted.

The bathroom was a lean-to affair of galvanized iron, containing a tin tub, three draughts, and a spider of unusual confidence. Cold water came through a pipe. Hot water had to be heated in the copper and carried in buckets. This discourages frivolous bathing, but gives serious bathing the dignity of an engineering project.

I lit the copper fire with shavings from the matchboard. My landlady objected to this.

“Those pieces might do for kindling,” she wrote.

“They are doing for kindling,” I replied.

She meant on some later, more deserving occasion. She stored scraps of wood with religious devotion and would save a broken clothes-peg from a burning house.

While the copper heated, I swept the bathroom and shook out the canvas bathing-cover I had designed myself. It fastened over the tub by cords and trapped the steam, leaving only the bather’s head exposed. A Turkish bath for the independent working man. I had improved it since its first trial with a short length of gas-pipe across the head end, supporting a folded towel so the neck rested comfortably and the skull did not knock against tin.

I tested the pipe. Firm.

I tightened the cords. Sound.

I hung a bath towel within reach, then moved it farther from the wall because galvanized iron has a peculiar gift for making a clean towel dirty. Beside it I placed a smaller towel for the face, because a man who wipes his face on the towel used for his feet may call himself practical, but he is merely impatient.

Next came soap, nailbrush, pumice stone, toothbrush, tooth powder, comb, and the little knife with which I cleaned paint from beneath my nails. I set out clean underclothes, shirt, trousers, socks, and slippers in the adjoining room, arranged in the order required. There is no pleasure in stepping from a hot bath and searching, naked and steaming, for the second sock.

I then considered intellectual refreshment.

A newspaper would collapse in the damp. A book was better, but not a valuable one. I chose an old volume of travel in Central Africa, its binding already beyond injury. There is something cooling in reading about a man short of water. I placed it on a fruit box beside the tub, together with tobacco, papers, matches sealed in a jam tin, and an ashtray made from the lid of a boot-polish tin.

The coffee required thought. If prepared too soon, it would cool; too late, and the bath would wait. I ground the beans—not because I was luxurious, but because someone had given me beans and I had no wish to waste them—set the pot on the stove, cut bread, toasted it, buttered it, and covered it with a plate. I added two slices of cold mutton and a little pickle. Bathing produces an appetite, and appetite, like rent, should be anticipated.

By then the copper was boiling. Steam lifted from it in splendid white rolls.

I carried the first bucket along the passage. Boiling water has a malicious intelligence. It waits until a man is passing a polished doorpost, then leaps upon his trousers. I moved slowly, one hand on the handle and the other beneath it with a folded rag. Into the tub it went, striking the tin with a grand, hollow crash which I felt through the floorboards.

The second bucket followed.

Then the third.

Between journeys I fed the copper, because three buckets were not enough. The tub was long, and I am not short. A cramped bath leaves the knees cold, which divides the body against itself.

My landlady appeared and wrote, “YOU WILL DROWN.”

I laughed. She looked hurt, rubbed out DROWN, and wrote, “YOU WILL SCALD YOURSELF.”

I pointed to the cold tap. She departed unconvinced, taking with her two unburned shavings from beside the copper.

I carried bucket after bucket. The heat in the passage was terrific; my dirty shirt clung to me; my arms began to tremble. Yet the anticipation was exquisite. Already I could imagine the steam closing around me, the canvas holding the warmth, the coffee at my elbow, Africa open upon my knees, my repaired fence standing firm in the night.

At last I judged there was sufficient hot water. I turned on the cold tap for a measured time, testing the stream with my wrist. A bath should be hot enough to make entry a negotiation, but not so hot that a man comes out the colour of corned beef.

I shut the tap.

I carried in the coffee, toast, mutton, and pickle. I adjusted the lamp. I opened the book at a chapter called “Disaster at the Salt Marsh.” Too ominous, I thought, and turned instead to “Among Friendly Tribes.” I rolled a cigarette in advance. I checked the clean clothes. I tested the gas-pipe once more.

Everything was ready.

I undressed in the kitchen because the bathroom floor was wet—why it was so wet did not occur to me—and left my filthy clothes in a heap. Then I walked in, lifted the canvas, and put one foot into the tub.

My foot struck cold tin.

There was no water.

For several seconds I stood there with one leg in the bath and one leg out, an attitude neither dignified nor safe. I looked at the tub. I looked at the wet floor. I looked at the little dark hole near my toes.

I’d forgotten to put in the plug.

All that water—the copperfuls, the buckets, the measured cold, the heat I had carried so carefully through the house—had passed straight down the pipe and into the yard. Outside, beneath the bathroom, a flourishing stream ran among the weeds. The spider alone had benefited.

I could have begun again. There was wood, though my landlady would have disputed it. There was water. There was still an hour before bedtime.

But the spirit had gone out of the undertaking. That is a real thing, the spirit of an undertaking. You cannot relight it with matchboard.

I stood looking at the soap, the brush, the tooth powder, the towels, the book, the tobacco protected in its jam tin, the coffee cooling beside the toast. Each object had become an accusation. Even the friendly tribes seemed sarcastic.

My landlady came to the doorway. She saw the empty tub, the water creeping across the floor, and me standing there in the altogether. Her face expressed such enormous sympathy that I resented her more than if she had laughed.

She wrote nothing.

I put on my dirty clothes again. That was the worst of it. Paint, rust, sweat, and the black substance from under the washhouse—all resumed their former positions. I drank the coffee standing up, ate half the toast without tasting it, stumbled to my room, and lay on the bed fully dressed.

I slept the sleep of utter defeated weariness.

In the morning I went onto the balcony. Mercy Terrace was pale under the early sun. At Number Four, a family was moving out. The father carried a rolled mattress; the mother held a saucepan and a cage without a bird. Their little boy dragged a wooden horse with only three wheels. They had arrived a month before with curtains, a clock, and two geraniums in tins. The geraniums were dead now. The clock had vanished earlier in the week.

The man paused and looked back at the house with an expression I understood too well.

People say such families are careless. Sometimes they are. So am I. They say the poor do not plan. But I have seen them plan down to the last shilling: rent here, food there, boots postponed, medicine halved, firewood borrowed, pride patched with brown paper. Everything considered. Everything arranged.

And then the work stops. Or a child falls ill. Or a landlord wants the room. Or a man has weak lungs, a bad leg, failing eyes—or ears that never heard properly in the first place. One little necessity is missing, perhaps through neglect, perhaps because life never supplied it.

The water runs away.

That is the moral, if you want one. A man may prepare his towels, warm his coffee, mend his fence, choose his book, and labour with intelligence and hope; but success sometimes depends upon one small plug, and it is unkind to laugh too loudly at those who discover, tired and naked, that theirs was never in the tub.

free_generation.response_text:
The Bell at Low Water

Every morning at six, Mara Vale climbed the lighthouse stairs with a brass key in one hand and a cup of black tea in the other.

There were one hundred and twelve steps. She knew where the stone was chipped on the thirty-seventh, where the iron rail grew coldest on the sixty-fourth, and where the tower leaned just enough to make the final turn feel steeper than the rest. At the top, she unlocked the glass chamber, extinguished the lamp, and watched daylight spread over the sea.

For twenty-three years, this had been her work.

The lighthouse stood on Saint Orra, a narrow island shaped like a sleeping dog. A village occupied the sheltered eastern side, while the western cliffs faced the open ocean. In winter, waves struck those cliffs hard enough to shake spoons in kitchen drawers. In summer, the water shone blue and mild, and visitors came on the ferry to buy postcards, eat crab soup, and complain that there was no signal for their telephones.

Mara lived alone in the keeper’s cottage. Her husband, Tomas, had vanished at sea fourteen years earlier. His boat had been found with its sail torn and its mast broken, but his body had never returned.

On Saint Orra, the missing were treated differently from the dead.

The dead had stones in the churchyard. Their names collected lichen. People brought flowers, said prayers, and eventually learned to speak of them in the past tense.

The missing had no place to rest. They remained in doorways, in weather reports, in empty chairs. They were always about to come home.

For the first seven years, Mara watched every sail.

For the next seven, she told herself she did not.

On a gray morning in October, as she reached the ninety-eighth step, she heard a bell ringing beneath the sea.

She stopped.

The sound came faintly through the lighthouse walls.

One clear note.

Then another.

Mara held her breath. The island church had one bell, but this sound did not come from the village. It rose from somewhere west of the cliffs, low and deep, with a long trembling echo.

She climbed to the lamp room and looked out.

The tide was at its lowest. Black rocks curved through the water like the spine of a buried animal. Beyond them, fog lay across the horizon.

The bell rang a third time.

Mara set down her tea.

She knew the old story. Everyone on Saint Orra did.

Long before the lighthouse, there had been another island west of the cliffs. It was called Merrow, and it had fields, wells, a chapel, and thirty houses roofed in red clay. One winter night, after weeks of storms, the sea rose over it. By morning, Merrow was gone.

According to the story, its chapel bell still rang at low water. Some said it warned of shipwreck. Others said it called the drowned home. Children were told never to follow it, because those who did would walk into the sea and keep walking until the water closed over their heads.

Mara had never believed the story. She had heard wind in sea caves, chains knocking against harbor posts, and buoys tolling miles away. The ocean made strange music, especially when people were eager to hear it.

Still, that morning, she searched the water until her tea went cold.

At the base of the tower, she found Eli Cress waiting beside the door.

Eli was ten years old, thin as a mast, and always missing one button from his coat. His grandmother ran the island shop. His father worked on cargo ships and returned twice a year with foreign coins, carved animals, and promises to remain ashore next time.

“Did you hear it?” Eli asked.

“Hear what?”

“The bell.”

Mara locked the lighthouse door. “Probably the western buoy.”

“The western buoy broke loose in March.”

“Then perhaps it came back.”

“It washed up in Dunley,” Eli said. “Mr. Pell saw it when he went for his teeth.”

Mara gave him a sharp look, but his face was solemn.

“Sound travels oddly in fog,” she said.

“There isn’t any fog here.”

“There is beyond the rocks.”

Eli considered this, then followed her down the path.

“What does it mean?”

“It means you’re late for school.”

“It rang three times.”

“Then you’re three times late.”

She expected him to grin. He did not.

At the village school, the teacher had also heard the bell. So had the baker, the harbor master, two fishermen, and old Nessa Crow, who claimed she remembered it ringing in 1958, just before a passenger ship struck the northern reef.

By noon, the entire island was talking about it.

Mara spent the afternoon checking weather instruments. Pressure was dropping, but not dangerously. The forecast promised rain and moderate winds from the southwest. She inspected the emergency generator, polished the lamp lenses, and tested the radio.

Everything worked.

At sunset, she lit the great lamp. Its beam swept across the darkening water in steady white intervals.

Far offshore, something flashed in answer.

Mara leaned toward the glass.

There it was again: a small yellow light, low on the western horizon.

She took up the binoculars. The sea was roughening, lifting in long steel-colored swells. The light disappeared behind them, then returned.

A boat, she thought.

But no vessel had been reported nearby, and the yellow glow did not move north or south. It remained fixed beyond the drowned rocks of Merrow.

Mara reached for the radio.

Before her fingers touched it, the bell rang.

The note rolled through the tower, stronger than before.

The yellow light went out.

The next morning, Eli was waiting again.

“My grandmother says Merrow comes back when it wants something,” he announced.

“Is that so?”

“She says it borrows the bell from the dead.”

Mara swept rainwater from the cottage step. “Your grandmother also says cold potatoes cure warts.”

“They cured mine.”

“You never had a wart.”

“That proves how well they worked.”

This time Mara smiled despite herself.

Eli looked toward the western cliffs. “I saw a light last night.”

“So did I.”

His eyes widened. “What was it?”

“I don’t know.”

“Can we go and see?”

“No.”

“At low tide, there’s a path.”

“There are rocks. Slippery ones.”

“Jory Flint went halfway last summer.”

“Jory Flint also put a live crab in the church collection box.”

“He said it was all he had.”

Mara rested the broom against the wall. “Listen to me. The western shore is dangerous, especially with the pressure falling. Stay away from it.”

Eli scuffed his boot against the ground. “My father was supposed to come home yesterday.”

Mara’s irritation faded.

“Which ship?”

“The North Lark. It reached Bellhaven, but he wasn’t on it. Gran says he probably changed routes.”

“Probably.”

“He didn’t send word.”

Mara knew what silence could grow into. At first it was a small empty space. Then it became a room, then a house, then a country in which a person might live for years.

“Cargo schedules change,” she said. “Radios fail. Men forget to send messages.”

“Did Tomas forget?”

The question struck with childish accuracy.

Eli immediately looked ashamed. “I’m sorry.”

Mara picked up the broom. “Go to school.”

He went.

All day, rain crossed the island in silver curtains. At three in the afternoon, the ferry canceled its evening journey. At four, the mainland weather office issued a gale warning.

Mara climbed to the lamp room before dusk. The wind had turned west and was rising fast. White water broke over the outer rocks. She lit the lamp early and watched its beam cut through rain.

At six, the harbor master called.

“Small boat missing out of Bellhaven,” he said. “Single mast, blue hull. Man aboard, perhaps two. They think it headed east yesterday.”

“Name?”

“Morning Rose.”

Mara closed her eyes.

Tomas’s boat had been named Morning Rose.

For one absurd second, fourteen years vanished. She saw him in the cottage doorway, hair wet with rain, laughing because he had forgotten his key. She smelled tar and salt on his coat.

“Mara?” said the harbor master.

“I’m here.”

“Not the same boat,” he said gently. “That one was never recovered from the north beach after they found it.”

“I know.”

“This one belongs to a fellow named Senn. Purchased it six years ago.”

“Who is missing?”

“Unclear. We’ll call when we know.”

By seven, the gale struck.

Wind howled around the tower. Rain hissed against the glass. Mara kept the lamp turning and monitored the radio, but the storm filled every frequency with static.

At half past eight, the bell began to ring.

Not three times.

Again and again it sounded beneath the storm, each note shuddering up through the rock. The tower seemed to vibrate with it.

Mara pressed her palms to the glass and stared west.

For a moment, the lamp’s beam swept across nothing but rain. Then it returned, and she saw the yellow light.

It was closer now.

It hovered beyond the black rocks, bright as a lantern carried by an invisible hand.

The radio cracked.

A boy’s voice whispered through the static.

“Mara?”

She seized the receiver. “Eli?”

Only noise answered.

“Eli, where are you?”

“Mara, I found—”

The signal broke.

She tried again, calling the harbor, the shop, anyone. No reply came.

Then the lighthouse door slammed far below.

Mara left the lamp room and ran down the stairs. She nearly fell at the thirty-seventh step and struck her shoulder against the wall. At the bottom, the entrance stood open, wind driving rain into the tower.

On the floor lay Eli’s cap.

She picked it up. It was soaked.

Outside, a flashlight flickered on the path toward the western cliffs.

Mara shouted his name, but the wind tore it away.

She pulled on her oilskin coat, took a coil of rope from the emergency cupboard, and followed.

The western path was little more than a pale scar through the grass. Rain blinded her. Twice she lost sight of the flashlight; twice it reappeared farther ahead.

At the cliff edge, she found Eli standing beside the old descent, a steep trail used generations ago by people gathering mussels. He was staring down at the shore.

The tide had retreated farther than Mara had ever seen.

Between the cliff and the outer rocks, the sea floor lay exposed. A road of flat stones ran westward through shallow water.

Beyond it, under the sweep of the lighthouse beam, rooftops rose from the sea.

Mara could not move.

Dark walls, broken chimneys, and narrow streets emerged between veils of rain. At the far end stood a chapel. Its steeple leaned, and within it swung a bell green with age.

Merrow.

The drowned island stretched before them.

Small lights glowed in its windows.

“I heard my father,” Eli said.

Mara grabbed his arm. “We’re going back.”

“He called from the chapel.”

“It isn’t him.”

“You don’t know.”

“Yes,” Mara said, though she did not. “I do.”

A figure appeared on the stone road.

It carried a yellow lantern.

The figure moved slowly toward them, sometimes hidden by waves spilling across the path. It wore a fisherman’s coat and a dark wool hat.

Mara stopped breathing.

She knew that walk.

Tomas had favored his left leg after a rope injury when he was seventeen. In bad weather, the limp became more pronounced. The approaching figure leaned exactly as he had.

“Mara,” it called.

His voice had not aged.

The years inside her split open.

She remembered their last morning: Tomas at the table, eating bread with honey; Tomas complaining about a frayed sail; Tomas kissing her cheek while she looked at a lighthouse maintenance list and told him to buy lamp oil on the mainland.

She had not watched him leave.

For fourteen years, she had revised that morning until it became a punishment. If she had looked up. If she had noticed the pressure dropping. If she had asked him to stay. If she had said goodbye properly.

Now he was walking toward her through the rain.

“Mara,” he called again. “Come help me.”

Eli pulled against her grip. “There! Someone’s behind him.”

A second lantern appeared near the chapel.

“Dad!” Eli shouted.

The boy wrenched free and started down the trail.

Mara caught him by the collar.

He kicked and twisted. “Let go!”

“No.”

“He needs me!”

“So does your grandmother.”

“My father’s there!”

“Tomas is there,” Mara said, and the words nearly broke her. “But Tomas is dead.”

The figure on the road stopped.

The bell rang.

All across drowned Merrow, doors opened.

People stepped into the streets.

There were dozens of them: men in old coats, women in long skirts, children barefoot in the rain. Some looked swollen and pale. Others seemed as warm and solid as the living. All turned their faces toward the cliff.

All began calling names.

The storm filled with voices.

Mothers heard lost children. Widows heard husbands. The old heard friends from youth. Mara heard her own name in Tomas’s voice, tender and impatient.

“You left the lamp,” he called. “Come home.”

Eli sagged against her. “What do we do?”

Mara tied one end of the rope around his waist and the other around hers.

“We climb.”

They had taken only a few steps when part of the cliff gave way.

Mud and stone slid beneath them. Eli fell. Mara dropped to one knee, braced against a rock, and held the rope as the boy swung over the edge.

He screamed.

Below him, waves poured across the exposed road. The dead moved closer.

Mara wrapped the rope around her forearm and pulled. Her shoulder burned where she had struck the lighthouse wall.

“Climb!” she shouted.

“I can’t!”

“Use your feet!”

Eli found a ledge. Mara hauled again. For a moment, his head rose above the edge.

Then Tomas spoke behind her.

“You can’t save everyone.”

She looked back.

He stood only a few yards away.

She had not seen him climb the trail. Water streamed from his coat. His face was the face she remembered—weathered, brown-eyed, a thin scar beneath the chin. In his hand, he held the yellow lantern.

“You tried,” he said. “That is enough.”

Mara’s grip weakened.

He smiled, and she saw the small gap between his front teeth.

No ghost invented by grief should have known that smile. No trick of storm and shadow should have known how he touched two fingers to his brow when he was worried.

“I waited,” she whispered.

“I know.”

“I kept the lamp.”

“I know.”

“Why didn’t you come home?”

Tomas looked toward the sea. “I could not.”

Below them, Eli sobbed and clawed at the rock.

Tomas held out his hand. “You can stop waiting now.”

Mara wanted to take it.

She wanted rest more than she had ever admitted. She wanted to walk down the stone road and enter one of those lit houses. She wanted a kitchen untouched by years, a kettle singing, Tomas’s boots by the door. She wanted to become the woman she had been on the morning before the sea divided her life.

The rope slipped another inch.

Eli cried out.

Mara looked at Tomas’s open hand.

Then she remembered something.

On the morning he vanished, he had not eaten bread with honey. They had been out of honey. He had spread plum jam on his bread and complained that the jar had gone moldy, though it had not.

For fourteen years, she had remembered the scene incorrectly.

Grief had polished it, sweetened it, made it shine.

The thing before her was not Tomas. It was the shape of waiting.

Mara tightened her grip on the rope.

“You are not my husband.”

The figure’s smile disappeared.

Behind him, the dead fell silent.

Mara pulled.

Pain flared through her shoulder and down her back. Eli kicked against the cliff, found another ledge, and rose. She caught his wrist and dragged him onto the grass.

Tomas lunged.

The yellow lantern went out.

For one instant, his face changed. Skin peeled into gray water. His eyes became empty sockets filled with sand. Seaweed hung from his teeth.

Then the lighthouse beam swept over him, and he vanished.

Mara and Eli crawled uphill.

Below, the tide returned.

It did not creep. It charged.

Waves crashed across the stone road and shattered against the drowned houses. Merrow’s lights went out one by one. The bell rang wildly as water climbed the chapel walls.

The dead called again, but their voices grew faint.

Mara did not look back.

They reached the lighthouse as the first wave struck the base of the western cliff. Inside, she bolted the door, untied the rope, and wrapped Eli in an old blanket.

“The lamp,” she said.

They climbed together.

The mechanism had stopped turning.

Perhaps Mara had failed to wind it fully. Perhaps the violence of the bell had shaken something loose. The great lens stood still, its beam fixed uselessly toward the north.

Mara opened the machinery panel.

A drive chain had slipped from its gear.

She reached inside, but her injured shoulder refused to lift. Eli pushed the sleeve of his coat above his elbows.

“Tell me what to do.”

Together they reset the chain. Mara guided his hands while he forced the metal over the gear teeth. Then she wound the mechanism, each turn sending fire through her arm.

At last, the lens began to move.

The beam swept west.

A blue-hulled boat appeared among the rocks.

Its mast was broken. Its sail dragged in the water. A man clung to the stern while waves drove the vessel toward the reef.

“Morning Rose,” Mara whispered.

Eli pressed himself to the glass. “Dad!”

The man looked up, though he could not have heard.

A rescue boat could not leave Saint Orra’s harbor in such seas. Mara radioed the mainland and fired the lighthouse emergency flare. Red light opened above the water.

The blue boat was too close to the rocks.

“Can he steer?” Eli asked.

“Maybe.”

Mara adjusted the auxiliary signal lamp. With the main beam showing the reef, she flashed the old harbor code across the water.

Three short. One long. Two short.

Safe passage east.

For several seconds, nothing happened.

Then the man at the stern moved. He pulled himself toward the tiller. A wave spun the boat sideways, but another lifted it clear of the first rock.

Mara sent the signal again.

Three short. One long. Two short.

The boat turned.

It entered the narrow channel between the reefs just as the tide swallowed the last stone of the road to Merrow.

By dawn, the gale had passed.

The Morning Rose grounded on the eastern beach, damaged but afloat. Two men were aboard. One was the boat’s owner, Senn, who had broken his leg. The other was Eli’s father.

He had missed his cargo ship after helping Senn repair the boat in Bellhaven. When the weather changed, they had tried to reach Saint Orra rather than return against the wind. Their radio failed before they could send word.

Eli ran into the shallows and threw himself against his father.

Mara watched from the beach, her arm in a sling.

Later, when the doctor had examined everyone and the villagers had finished telling the story incorrectly, Eli found her beside the lighthouse.

“Was that really Merrow?” he asked.

Mara looked west.

The sea was blue and calm. Gulls circled over the rocks. Nothing remained of the road, the houses, or the chapel.

“Yes,” she said.

“Was that really Tomas?”

“No.”

Eli waited.

Mara considered her answer.

“Perhaps part of it was,” she said. “The part I wouldn’t let go.”

“Will the bell ring again?”

“Probably.”

“What should we do if it does?”

Mara put the brass key into the lighthouse door.

“We listen,” she said. “But we don’t follow.”

Winter passed. The story of the storm traveled to the mainland and returned enlarged. Newspapers wrote about an optical illusion caused by unusual tides. A university sent two researchers to examine the western rocks. They found fragments of red roof tile, a rusted hinge, and a bronze clapper from a bell.

The people of Saint Orra were not surprised.

In spring, Mara cleared Tomas’s clothes from the wooden chest at the foot of her bed. She gave his heavy coat to Eli’s father, his boots to the harbor master, and his wool hats to the church charity.

At the bottom of the chest, she found a jar wrapped in cloth.

Plum jam.

The seal had broken years ago. Inside, the fruit had dried into a dark, sweet crust.

Mara laughed until she cried.

Then she buried the jar beneath the apple tree and placed a flat stone over it. She carved no name. She did not need to. It was not a grave, only a place to set down what she had carried too long.

Years later, when Mara’s hair had turned white and Eli was old enough to serve as assistant keeper, the bell rang again at low water.

They stood together in the lamp room.

Out beyond the western rocks, a yellow light moved through the dusk.

Eli glanced at Mara.

“Do you hear anyone?” he asked.

She listened.

The bell’s note traveled through water and stone. Beneath it rose a confusion of distant voices, gentle as rain on glass. Once, she thought she heard Tomas laugh. The sound no longer pulled at her. It passed through her like wind through an open house.

“No,” she said.

It was almost true.

Together, they lit the lamp.

Its beam crossed the dark water, turned over the place where Merrow slept, and continued toward the horizon.
